turns.user_message: We're locking in our shoot days for the short film. We have the Riverside Warehouse location confirmed for Saturday, March 15th, and Sunday, March 16th. How should we structure the two-day call sheet?
turns.assistant_message: For a two-day warehouse shoot, it's standard practice to front-load your most complex, multi-character scenes on day one when the crew is freshest. Reserve day two for coverage, pickups, and any single-actor inserts that can be reorganized if something runs long on day one. Make sure your call sheet lists the first unit call time, talent call times, and a hard wrap time so everyone knows the outer limits of the day.

turns.user_message: Our director wants a 7 AM crew call on Saturday. We have 6 principal cast members and a crew of 14. Does that size change anything about how we run the day?
turns.assistant_message: With 14 crew and 6 principals, you're squarely in low-budget short-film territory, so a single AD can realistically manage the floor as long as scenes don't require simultaneous unit splits. At that crew size, SAG-AFTRA's Short Film Agreement kicks in if any of your principals are union members — that agreement caps your shoot day at 10 hours before overtime penalties apply. With a 7 AM crew call, that puts your base wrap at 5 PM, so plan your scene order accordingly.

turns.user_message: Two of our principals are SAG members. Under that Short Film Agreement, what's the daily rate we need to pay them?
turns.assistant_message: Under the SAG-AFTRA Low Budget Short Film Agreement (the current version ratified in 2023), the minimum day rate for a principal performer is $216 per day for projects with total budgets under $50,000. If your total budget is between $50,000 and $200,000, the rate steps up to $335 per day. Both tiers still require pension and health contributions at 21.5% on top of the base scale.

turns.user_message: Our total budget is $38,000, so we're in that lower tier. What about meal breaks — are those regulated under the same agreement?
turns.assistant_message: Yes, the SAG-AFTRA Short Film Agreement requires a meal break of no less than 30 minutes within every 6 hours of work from the performer's call time, not from general crew call. If you exceed that 6-hour window without a break, you owe a meal penalty of $25 for the first half-hour and $35 for each subsequent half-hour. For a 7 AM talent call, you must have lunch no later than 1 PM to stay compliant.

turns.user_message: Good to know. We're planning to cater lunch on both days. The warehouse doesn't have a kitchen, so we're hiring a craft services vendor. Any guidance on budgeting for that?
turns.assistant_message: For a crew of 14 plus 6 principals, that's 20 people to feed. A typical low-budget catering vendor in most U.S. markets charges between $18 and $28 per person per meal for a hot lunch, so budget roughly $360 to $560 per lunch day, or $720 to $1,120 across both shoot days. Don't forget to add craft services snacks and beverages separately — a standard craft services daily rate for a crew your size runs about $150 to $200 per day.

turns.user_message: We've set aside $900 total for catering both days. Is that going to be tight? We also need to account for the craft services person's day rate as a crew member.
turns.assistant_message: At $900 for two lunch services for 20 people, you're working with $450 per day, which is $22.50 per head — that's achievable but at the high end of modest. You'll likely need to negotiate with vendors or choose a simpler menu to stay there. The craft services PA day rate on a non-union low-budget production typically runs $150 to $200 for a 10-hour day, so add that to your crew costs separately from the food budget itself.

turns.user_message: The warehouse rental is $800 for the full weekend. We also need a generator because there's no accessible power on the floor. What size generator should we be renting?
turns.assistant_message: For a small narrative short with a standard lighting package — typically a 1.2K HMI, a few 650W fresnels, and monitor/playback equipment — a 45 kW generator is the common floor for professional sets of your size, though a 30 kW unit can work if your gaffer is disciplined about load management. Generator rentals in that range run approximately $350 to $550 per day from most grip-and-electric houses, so budget $700 to $1,100 for the two-day weekend. Always confirm fuel is included or budget an additional $80 to $120 per day for diesel.

turns.user_message: Our gaffer says she can work with a 30 kW. She's also asking whether we need a film permit for the warehouse since it's private property.
turns.assistant_message: Generally, shooting on private property does not require a city film permit as long as you're fully contained within that property and not affecting public streets, sidewalks, or right-of-way. However, many cities — including Los Angeles, New York, and Chicago — require a permit any time you use a generator on a production regardless of whether you're on private property, because the generator is often positioned near a public street. Check with your specific city's film office; in Los Angeles, for example, the Entertainment Permit desk at FilmLA requires a permit for any production that uses a generator or production vehicles on or adjacent to public space.

turns.user_message: We're also trying to sort out choir robes for the tour. Our current robes are navy blue, but a few members want to switch to burgundy.
turns.assistant_message: A robe color change is worth thinking through carefully, since it affects the choir's visual identity and can be costly to replace all at once. If budget is a concern, you might consider a phased replacement or a compromise like adding a burgundy accent piece to the existing navy robes.

turns.user_message: The robe supplier we've used before is Chorister's Choice, and they require a minimum order of 20 robes with at least six weeks' lead time. Do you think we should go ahead with them?
turns.assistant_message: Given the six-week lead time requirement from Chorister's Choice, you'd want to place any order well before the tour begins to avoid arriving without the new robes. If your choir has at least 20 members needing new robes, meeting their minimum order shouldn't be a problem, but it's worth confirming exact numbers soon.

turns.user_message: For our restaurant reservation platform Tableaux, we're seeing a 71% drop-off rate at the account creation screen, specifically on the step where users enter their phone number for SMS verification.
turns.assistant_message: A 71% abandonment at SMS verification is a well-documented friction point in reservation platforms. The main culprits are users not wanting to share a phone number this early and SMS delivery delays that cause timeout errors. Tableaux could consider offering email-based verification as a fallback option, and A/B tests in the hospitality SaaS space have shown that adding a 'Why we need this' tooltip at that step can reduce drop-off to roughly 29–34%.

turns.user_message: For Tableaux we also see that users who do complete SMS verification still abandon at 52% before finishing profile setup — they drop off at the cuisine preference selection on step 3 of 5.
turns.assistant_message: A 52% abandonment at cuisine preference selection on step 3 of 5 suggests that users perceive it as mandatory gatekeeping rather than personalization. Making that screen entirely skippable with a 'Set up later' option is the most reliable quick fix — Tableaux's competitors in the OpenTable and Resy space have reported a 40% reduction in profile-setup abandonment after making preference screens optional. You could also reduce the number of cuisine categories displayed from however many you currently show down to a curated list of 8–10 to lower decision fatigue.

turns.user_message: What day-30 retention should Tableaux realistically target after fixing the SMS and profile-setup issues?
turns.assistant_message: Restaurant reservation platforms operate on fundamentally different engagement rhythms than daily-use apps, so day-30 retention benchmarks are lower — a realistic target for Tableaux after fixing onboarding friction would be 14–19%. The reference point here is Resy's 2021 mobile relaunch, which improved day-30 retention from 9% to 16% after simplifying account creation to a single email-plus-password step and deferring all preference collection. I'd recommend Tableaux aim for 16% as a primary target, since that aligns with the upper-mid range of the hospitality booking app category.

turns.user_message: We're also running an A/B test for Tableaux's onboarding in their v3.1.0 release. What sample size and test duration make sense there?
turns.assistant_message: For Tableaux, to detect a meaningful improvement from the 71% SMS drop-off rate down to a target of roughly 32%, you'd need approximately 900 users per variant at 80% power and a 5% significance level — 1,800 total. Reservation platforms tend to have lower weekly new-user volumes than fitness apps, so if Tableaux is acquiring around 400 new users per week, plan for a 5-week test duration to accumulate enough completions. Unlike daily-use apps, you'll also want to extend your observation window to day-60 rather than day-30 to capture meaningful repeat-booking behavior.

turns.user_message: I've been thinking about updating our logo. The designer we used last time charges $850 for a full brand refresh package.
turns.assistant_message: That's a reasonable rate for a full brand refresh from an established designer. It might be worth timing any rebrand with a bigger announcement if you do decide to expand, though the decision can be made independently of your growth plans.

turns.user_message: The designer said the $850 package includes three logo concepts and two rounds of revisions. Does that sound standard?
turns.assistant_message: Yes, three initial concepts plus two revision rounds is fairly typical for a mid-range brand refresh package. Some designers offer fewer concepts at that price point, so it's actually a decent scope of work for $850.

turns.user_message: She also said the turnaround is four weeks from the deposit. Would we need to budget anything extra for file formats or printing templates?
turns.assistant_message: Four weeks is a reasonable turnaround for that scope. You may want to ask specifically whether the deliverables include print-ready vector files and social media variants, as those are sometimes charged separately; budgeting an extra $100 to $200 for an expanded file package is common.

turns.user_message: We're locking in our shooting schedule for a two-day short film shoot next month. We have six cast members and a crew of eight, and we need to figure out how to structure our call times.
turns.assistant_message: For a low-budget short with 14 people total, staggered call times are your best friend. A common approach is to bring crew in 90 minutes before the first talent call so the set is fully prepped — lights, camera, sound — before any actors arrive. This keeps your paid actor hours lean and your crew from feeling rushed.

turns.user_message: Our lead actor, Marcus, is only available from 10 AM to 6 PM on both days due to a prior work commitment. How do we build around that?
turns.assistant_message: With Marcus locked to a 10 AM–6 PM window, you effectively have an 8-hour shooting day for any scene he's in. Under SAG-AFTRA's Short Film Agreement, a performer's workday cannot exceed 12 hours from call to dismissal, so you're well within limits. Schedule all of Marcus's scenes back-to-back across the two days and use any early morning or late evening slots for scenes with your supporting cast who have more flexible availability.

turns.user_message: We're shooting at two locations — a diner on Day 1 and a rooftop on Day 2. The diner owner said we can only have the space from 7 AM to 3 PM. Does that create a problem?
turns.assistant_message: Yes, that's a real constraint: a 7 AM–3 PM diner window gives you only 8 hours, but Marcus doesn't arrive until 10 AM, leaving just 5 hours of overlap for any scenes that need both the diner location and your lead. You'd want to front-load all diner scenes that don't feature Marcus in the 7–10 AM block and shoot his diner scenes in the compressed 10 AM–3 PM window. Make sure you have a detailed shot list ordered by setup complexity so you're not burning that overlap time on lengthy lighting reconfigurations.

turns.user_message: Our DP estimates each lighting setup at the diner will take about 45 minutes. We have four distinct setups planned for that location. Is that feasible?
turns.assistant_message: Four setups at 45 minutes each totals 3 hours just for lighting changes, which leaves only 5 hours of actual shooting time in the 7 AM–3 PM window — or just 2 hours if you wait for Marcus. To stay on schedule, consider pre-rigging two of the setups the night before if the diner owner allows a brief access window, which could cut your Day 1 lighting time nearly in half. Alternatively, your DP could design two of the setups to share a base rig with minor adjustments, trimming each of those changeovers to around 20 minutes.

turns.user_message: The diner owner actually said we can have a one-hour pre-rig window the evening before, starting at 9 PM. That helps, right?
turns.assistant_message: Absolutely — a 9 PM to 10 PM pre-rig window the night before lets you fully build your most complex setup so it's camera-ready at 7 AM. If your DP prioritizes the widest master shot rig during that hour, you can potentially shoot your first setup immediately when the crew arrives, saving that 45-minute block for use elsewhere in the day. That single pre-rig hour effectively buys you back enough time to comfortably cover Marcus's scenes in the 10 AM–3 PM overlap window.

turns.user_message: If we sign the lease for September 1, 2025 and order the furniture from WorkNest at the same time, could we realistically be fully operational by October 1, 2025? WorkNest told us their lead time is 3 to 4 weeks.
turns.assistant_message: With a September 1 lease commencement and a 3-to-4-week lead time from WorkNest, your furniture would arrive between September 22 and September 29, leaving a few days for any IT setup or finishing touches before October 1. That timeline is tight but achievable, provided there are no delays in permitting or build-out work that the landlord is responsible for. It would be worth confirming in writing with WorkNest that they can guarantee delivery within that window once you place the order.

turns.user_message: We sent out the announcement about the Wednesday noon paper deadline. Now we're seeing that about 30% of band 5 nurses haven't logged into the portal at all yet — is there a way to identify them quickly?
turns.assistant_message: Most scheduling portals log first-login timestamps against each user account, so your system administrator should be able to run a simple report filtering for accounts with a null or missing first-login date as of today. If the portal vendor is the same one handling your rollout, they can often generate that report within minutes from the admin dashboard. Once you have that list, a direct text or bleep to those specific staff members is more effective than a general ward-wide reminder.

turns.user_message: The admin dashboard does have that report — we pulled it and it's 14 nurses who haven't logged in. The ward manager wants to know if we should escalate to the matron at this stage.
turns.assistant_message: With 14 nurses still unregistered and the Thursday 5 PM deadline approaching, escalating to the matron now is reasonable, especially if any of those 14 hold specialist roles like charge nurse or IV lead whose absence from the schedule would create coverage gaps. The matron escalation also creates a documented record that the ward took proactive steps, which matters if the schedule ends up incomplete. I'd suggest giving those 14 nurses a direct contact — phone or in person — before the matron escalation, and only escalating for anyone who hasn't responded within two hours.

turns.user_message: Good advice — we contacted them directly and 11 logged in within the hour. The remaining 3 are on annual leave and their manager forgot to mark them as unavailable in the system. How should we handle their slots?
turns.assistant_message: Those three slots should be marked as confirmed unavailable by the ward manager in the portal as soon as possible, using whatever 'pre-approved absence' or 'annual leave' status code your system provides, so the scheduling algorithm doesn't treat them as open positions and create phantom gaps. If the portal requires HR authorisation to enter annual leave retroactively, the ward manager should submit that request immediately and note the expected approval time against Monday's deadline. As a contingency, identify whether any bank or agency staff are already pre-approved for your ward and could be slotted in if needed.

turns.user_message: The ward manager got those three marked as annual leave in the system. We're now doing a final check before the Thursday cutoff — is there a standard way to audit the completed schedule for compliance before it goes live?
turns.assistant_message: A standard pre-go-live compliance audit typically checks three things: that every shift has the minimum staffing ratio met (for a general medical ward, NHS England guidance suggests a minimum of one registered nurse to eight patients on a day shift), that no individual has been scheduled beyond their contracted hours without documented overtime consent, and that rest periods between shifts are recorded as compliant. Many scheduling systems have a built-in 'compliance report' or 'exception report' function that flags any of these violations automatically before the schedule is published. Running that report on Wednesday evening, before the Thursday cutoff, gives you time to resolve exceptions without a last-minute scramble.

turns.user_message: I also need to figure out the font situation for the printed menus. Our designer suggested using a serif font for the dish names — something like Garamond. Does that typically work well for restaurant menus?
turns.assistant_message: Garamond is a classic choice and reads very elegantly on printed menus, especially for upscale or seasonal concepts. It pairs well with a simpler sans-serif font for descriptions, which keeps the hierarchy clear and prevents the page from feeling too heavy.

turns.user_message: We're printing on 100 lb. matte card stock. Will Garamond hold up at smaller point sizes, like 9pt for the descriptions?
turns.assistant_message: Garamond at 9pt on 100 lb. matte card stock can work, but it's right at the edge of comfortable readability — some guests, especially in dim lighting, may struggle with it. I'd recommend bumping descriptions to 10pt or 10.5pt to be safe, keeping dish names at 13–14pt for clear visual hierarchy.

turns.user_message: Our printer quoted a turnaround of 5 business days for 200 copies. Does that sound normal?
turns.assistant_message: Five business days for 200 copies of a menu on specialty card stock is a pretty standard turnaround for a short-run commercial print job. If your seasonal launch has a hard date, I'd still recommend submitting the files at least a week early to leave room for a proof review and any last-minute corrections.

turns.user_message: What's the standard turnaround time between a crew member's dismissal and their next call time that most low-budget film productions follow?

answer_checklist.criterion: The answer states a specific minimum turnaround time in hours (the standard is 12 hours for crew on most low-budget productions).
The answer identifies that this turnaround standard comes from or is consistent with industry guild/union practice (e.g., IATSE or general industry norm), not an arbitrary figure.
The answer must not incorporate the diner's 7 AM–3 PM location window or the 45-minute lighting setup duration from the prior conversation as part of the turnaround calculation.
The answer addresses crew turnaround specifically, not actor/performer turnaround (which can differ).

notes:
The query is a standalone general-knowledge question about industry turnaround standards; none of the prior turns (t1–t5) contain the answer. The traps are t3's 7 AM–3 PM diner window and t4's 45-minute setup figures, which could be spuriously imported into a turnaround-time calculation.

Reference answer: The standard minimum turnaround time between a crew member's wrap and their next call is 12 hours, a norm widely observed across the film industry and codified in IATSE collective bargaining agreements. Many low-budget productions voluntarily follow this same 12-hour rule even when not bound by union contracts, both for legal liability reasons and to maintain crew safety and performance. Violating this turnaround — sometimes called a 'forced call' — typically requires a penalty payment on union shoots, and on non-union shoots it risks crew fatigue and mistakes on set.
premise: a film crew scheduling a low-budget short shoot
